candidates.attacker_control: Any application path that lets an attacker supply an XML document to the public `filter+xml` input filter (component XMLInputFilterFactory) or otherwise call XMLParserFactory.parse with attacker XML can control filter block names, parameter element names, and the `t` type attribute. The default XMLConfiguration uses `t` as the parameter type attribute. A valid filter element/parameter pair causes the attacker's class name and child XML to be processed by Class.forName and XStream.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The `t` attribute is an intentional serialization feature used to preserve concrete parameter types, and values are limited to classes visible to the current class loader. No concrete gadget class was verified in this snapshot, and no in-repository caller of XMLParserFactory.parse was found outside the filter+xml pipeline, so downstream exposure is required. XStream 1.4.17 may reject some known dangerous classes through built-in default restrictions, and XStream conversion can fail without side effects for some selected classes. No code was executed to confirm exploitability.
candidates.impact: Arbitrary class loading/initialization and attacker-controlled object graph deserialization. If a usable XStream gadget is on the classpath, this can escalate to remote code execution. Even without a gadget, it can cause unexpected object construction, type confusion, and denial of service. Because this is a reusable filter-parsing API, the impact applies to any downstream product that parses untrusted XML with it.
candidates.prerequisites: 1) Downstream code must expose a filter conversion/parsing operation accepting attacker-supplied XML and using the `filter+xml` input factory (or call XMLParserFactory.parse directly). 2) The XML must use a block/parameter combination recognized by the configured target output filter. 3) A suitable gadget or side-effecting class must be present on the application classpath for RCE; without a gadget the issue still permits arbitrary class initialization, arbitrary object instantiation/field population, and denial of service. No attacker authentication is enforced by this library code; authorization is entirely the caller's responsibility.
candidates.root_cause: DefaultXMLParser.unserializeParameter() reads the parameter type attribute (default name "t") directly from untrusted XML, loads it with Class.forName(typeString, true, ...), and passes the resulting class to XStreamParameterManager.unSerialize(). That manager uses ParameterXStream/NoWarningXStream, a plain XStream subclass with no type allowlist or security mapper, so the XML content controls the concrete class that XStream instantiates and populates. There is no check that the selected type is the expected parameter type, a subtype, or an allowed type.
candidates.title: Attacker-selected class instantiation/XStream deserialization in filter XML parameter parsing
candidates.trace: XML source -> XMLInputFilterFactory (filter+xml) creates DefaultXMLInputFilterStream -> AbstractXMLInputFilterStream.read() -> XMLInputFilterStreamUtils.createXMLEventReader() -> XMLInputFilterFactory.createXMLEventWriter() -> DefaultXMLParserFactory.createXMLEventWriter() -> SAXEventWriter(DefaultXMLParser). On endElement, DefaultXMLParser builds a DOM for the parameter, calls setParameter(block, filterParameter, Element), and then unserializeParameter(). If the XML element has the configured type attribute (`t`), DefaultXMLParser calls Class.forName(attackerValue, true, TCCL) and passes the class plus the attacker-controlled DOM to XStreamParameterManager.unSerialize(). XStreamParameterManager calls `new ParameterXStream(...).unmarshal(new DomReader(rootElement), null, dataHolder)`, and ParameterXStream has no addPermission/allowTypes/security mapper setup, so XStream instantiates the selected class and populates its fields from attacker XML.
candidates.unverified: Whether the actual XWiki Platform/downstream application exposes `filter+xml` XML parsing to untrusted users was not verifiable from this repository alone, and no concrete gadget chain or runtime RCE was demonstrated. The exact XML block/parameter shape needed for a specific output filter was not built or tested.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-502: Deserialization of Untrusted Data (also CWE-470 unsafe reflection)

coverage_summary: Inspected the repository-relative source tree exposed for this run: 1,425 model-visible text files across xwiki-commons-core and xwiki-commons-tools. I reviewed XML parsing/serialization (xwiki-commons-xml, filter-xml, filter-stream-xml, extension descriptors), XStream usage (xwiki-commons-xstream, job status/history/logging), job status storage, extension/local storage path handling, Netflux WebSocket endpoint, Velocity tools/introspection, HTML cleaning/sanitization, environment/classloader URL handling, crypto store file naming, and XAR/tool plugins. Test sources are not present in the snapshot, so tests and test-only configuration were not reviewed. No code, tests, scanners, or exploit payloads were executed.
limitations: No runtime execution or dynamic analysis was performed; exploitability and gadget availability are unverified.
The snapshot contains no test sources, so tests and test-provided configuration were unavailable.

The repository is a library snapshot; the XWiki Platform and other downstream callers that may expose filter XML parsing, job status APIs, or Netflux are outside the source scope, so end-to-end attacker reachability for several leads is unproven.
Review was broad but not exhaustive line-by-line over all 1,425 files; some modules were sampled via targeted searches rather than fully read.

Parser behavior (Xerces DOMConfiguration features, Woodstox DTD defaults, XStream 1.4.17 default type restrictions) was inferred from source and general API behavior, not verified in this environment.

rejected_leads.lead: Path traversal in DefaultJobStatusStore job-folder encoding
rejected_leads.reason: DefaultJobStatusStore.encode() URL-encodes '/' but leaves '.' intact, unlike PathUtils.encode() which encodes dots. A job ID element of '..' can escape the status storage root and getJobStatus()/remove() can read or recursively delete outside it. However, remove() is only called by the deprecated DefaultJobStatusStorage in this snapshot, and no in-repository caller passes attacker-controlled job IDs; downstream exposure was not provable, so it is a strong secondary lead rather than the selected candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: SafeXStream has no type allowlist (setupDefaultSecurity commented out)
rejected_leads.reason: SafeXStream extends XStream and explicitly does not call setupDefaultSecurity, while JobStatusSerializer and extension job-history/log serializers call fromXML on files. This is a credible CWE-502 sink, but the in-repository paths are file-based and no attacker-controlled file write/read chain is visible here, so it is less directly evidenced than the XML filter parser sink.

XMLUtils.parse sets the 'disallow-doctype-decl' feature to false and does not use FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING; DefaultExtensionSerializer parses descriptors with a plain DocumentBuilderFactory; XMLInputFilterStreamUtils uses a StAX factory without explicitly disabling DTD/external entities. Effective exploitability depends on the parser implementation and other settings (XMLUtils.parse does disable external general/parameter entities), and no concrete in-repo untrusted caller was proven, so these remain unconfirmed leads.

rejected_leads.lead: HTML sanitizer default permits unknown URI protocols and CSS style values
rejected_leads.reason: SecureHTMLElementSanitizer defaults allowUnknownProtocols to true and treats style/data attributes specially, which may enable browser-specific bypasses or CSS-based attacks. No concrete XSS payload or browser execution path was established from source alone, so this is not evidence-strong enough to submit.

Utils.getRandomHexString uses java.util.Random for channel keys, user names, and the history-keeper key. This is a weak-randomness/capability issue, but exploitability requires predicting 48-bit-seeded values or knowing a channel key, and the endpoint appears to treat channel keys as capabilities; no concrete unauthorized-access chain was proven.

summary: Reviewed the XWiki Commons 14.10.5 snapshot (1,425 files) with emphasis on network/deserialization/XML/path-handling code. The strongest single candidate is an unsafe XStream deserialization sink in the generic XML filter parser: XML input can select an arbitrary Java class through the parameter type attribute, and the parameter is then unmarshalled with a permissive XStream instance. I did not find a fully self-contained remote exploit path in this library and did not execute or runtime-confirm anything.
